doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Can racism be legislated? Lynching history and real equality
summary: Answering Rowe, he says trust cannot be legislated, recounts Sweets Edison's lynching memory, and says he wants equal access to voting rather than reparations.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Human nature is scary sometimes and I wonder how we change — what has to change first, the attitude or is it something that just has to be legislated? That you can’t get away with acting like that anymore.

I think — I like your language of legislating but it’s interesting I was working with a friend of mine that’s a lawyer. I had gotten this contract for a gig and it had all this crazy language in it about what I was supposed to do. And he goes, “It appears they don’t trust you.” He said, “And you can’t write trust in a contract.” The things that you and I are talking about now, they can’t be legislated or put in a contract. They have to come from the heart. And as we’ve talked about this being a problem, you have to agree that there is a problem before you can begin to solve it, and I think that we’re at that point is that can we agree that something happened? Can we agree that — and I’ll go deep and dark now — can we agree that people, black people were hung from trees. Sweets Edison told me, he says, “You know when I used to walk by white women I would always look at my shoes because I didn’t want anybody to say ‘You’re looking at that white woman.’” Because I’d seen the lynchings. And so can we agree that lynchings happened? Some people will tell you the Holocaust didn’t happen. That’s how deep it gets, all right? So can we agree that lynchings happened? And can we agree that when they happened people would gather to watch those lynchings? And can we agree that I have pictures of people putting their kids on their shoulders to watch those things? And can we agree if you look at the audiences in those pictures that people were smiling and grinning? Can we agree that they would cut people’s fingers off and put them in jars and put them in the thing that preserves it, and they would sell them. They say, “You want a souvenir from the lynching?” Can we agree that people made postcards from the lynchings and on the back of one of them they wrote, “This was the bar-b-que that we had tonight.” Can I go even deeper and can we agree that there was this curiosity about the black man’s sexual prowess and so not only would you be lynched but before the lynching they would take your penis and cut it off and castrate you and many times stick it in your mouth. That’s a legacy that people don’t want to deal with. They want to tell you, boy you just need to be quiet when the policeman stops you. And as I said before, you could even be quiet, you still might get shot. So I think how do we begin to have uncomfortable conversations, crucial conversations. And I don’t want sympathy. I personally don’t want reparations. Because to me what reparations are, what they should be if there’s reparations, it’s just equality. So that the people in Kentucky don’t have to go 600,000 to one polling place. That’s the reparations I want. I want as many polling places as naturally accommodate that amount of people. And don’t tell me that that’s a fair election. Right?
